description: The record's 'River Woman (Zapotec)' is Lucía Zenteno, the radiant Zapotec woman of Oaxacan tradition so beautiful that the sun itself fell in love with her and carried her away. Her husband pursued her into the sky, but a jealous moon spirit parted them forever. The story, retold by Alejandro Cruz Martínez in 'The Woman Who Outshone the Sun' (1991), is Mexican, not North American.

The record's 'drowning, luring' traits do not belong to Lucía Zenteno, who is a figure of light and loss rather than a water spirit.

description: In Greenlandic Inuit tradition the raven (tulugaq) is a culture hero and bringer of light. In an origin tale recorded across the Arctic, a raven-child born of a woman steals the light a selfish being keeps in a box, flying it through the smoke hole and scattering stars and daylight across the sky. Raven also appears in Inuit stories as a creator and transformer.
source: Inuit origin-of-light cycle; Knud Rasmussen, Reports of the Fifth Thule Expedition (1921-24); Greenlandic oral tradition
research_notes: Tulugaq (raven) is genuine in Greenlandic Inuit folklore. The light-stealing myth is attested across Inuit groups; raven's creator/transformer role appears in several versions. The record's deity framing is a reasonable synthesis of the raven trickster-creator complex.

description: Tséghádiʼnídíinii atʼééd, Rock Crystal Girl, is a Navajo holy being who dwells with her brother Rock Crystal Boy at Sisnaajiní (Blanca Peak), the sacred mountain of the East. She was created by the Holy People when the six sacred mountains were re-established after the emergence into the Fourth World, embodying the white shell and crystal essence of dawn.
source: Diné Bahaneʼ (Navajo creation narrative); Kerry Thompson dissertation on Navajo sacred mountains; Washington Matthews, The Mountain Chant (1887)
research_notes: Attested. Rock Crystal Girl is a genuine resident deity of Sisnaajiní in Navajo tradition, paired with Rock Crystal Boy. The input's own description and summary already cite the correct mountain and creation context.

description: In the Jicarilla Apache creation narrative, Holy Boy (the record's 'Red Boy') is the younger companion of Killer-of-Enemies. research_notes: Attested. The Jicarilla Apache origin story features Holy Boy, who with Killer-of-Enemies secured the sun and moon. The record's 'Red Boy' naming is a variant; its 'in the beginning there was nothing' summary matches the Jicarilla opening.

description: Kâ'lanû Ahkyeli'skï, the Raven Mocker, is a malevolent Cherokee witch-spirit that preys on the dying. Ordinary people by day, Raven Mockers fly at night as shadowy birds with sleepless, bloodshot eyes, stealing the remaining years of the sick. Only medicine men and their allies can see them and drive them off with protective rituals, as James Mooney recorded.
source: James Mooney, Myths of the Cherokee (1900), 'The Raven Mocker'; Cherokee spiritual beliefs
research_notes: Attested and already well-documented (confirmed in prior batch work). Kâ'lanû Ahkyeli'skï is genuine Cherokee death-witch belief; Mooney's account matches the input's raven-witches preying on the dying.

description: Häki Suto, the Giant Cloud-Swallower, is a Zuni ogre who brought drought by drinking the clouds from the sky, so the rains failed and the people starved. In Zuni folk tales the War Twins pursued and slew him, freeing the clouds so the waters returned to the land, explaining drought and the restoration of rain through the twins' heroism.

description: In the Cherokee account of creation, the Great Buzzard flew over the soft, newly dried earth. Each downward beat of his enormous wings created a valley, each upward stroke a mountain, shaping the rolling landscape of the Cherokee homeland. The story, told in Mooney's 'How the World Was Made', explains the mountains and valleys of Cherokee country.
source: James Mooney, Myths of the Cherokee (1900), 'How the World Was Made' (sacred-texts.com motc000)
research_notes: Attested. The Great Buzzard is father of all buzzards in Cherokee tradition; his wing strikes made the valleys and mountains. Mooney's text confirms the input.

description: In Haida tradition the woman whose rising caused the great flood is a tide-controlling figure: mocked for her seaweed-like backbone, she sat at the water's edge and the tide rose with her until the whole island flooded, scattering the people on rafts to different lands. The episode appears in Swanton's Haida Texts and Myths and has been linked to post-glacial sea-level rise.
source: John R. Swanton, Haida Texts and Myths, BAE Bulletin 29 (1905), pp. 318-320; Haida oral tradition; Patrick Nunn, The Edge of Memory
research_notes: Attested as the Haida flood-tide woman. The exact modern spelling 'GaayhllGa Jaad' could not be confirmed letter-for-letter in Swanton's text (his orthography is phonetic), but the flood-myth episode is genuine and the modern Haida name is used in contemporary sources. A separate Low Tide Woman figure (Chaaw Jaadee) also exists.

description: In the Bear Mother legend shared by the Haida, Nisga'a, Gitxsan and Coast Tsimshian, a young woman who mocked the bears was taken as wife by the son of the Grizzly Bear chief and bore twin bear cubs. Her sons, born of a human and a bear, became ancestors and gave the people the bear as a clan crest and guardian spirit.
source: Bear Mother legend; SFU Bill Reid Centre for Northwest Coast Art Studies; Haida/Nisga'a/Gitxsan oral tradition
research_notes: Attested as a shared Northwest Coast legend rather than a distinct named 'Grizzly Bear Spirit.' The Bear Mother story is genuine Haida tradition, and the bear figures prominently as a clan crest and supernatural guardian. Bill Reid's 'Spirit of Haida Gwaii' depicts the Bear Mother's boat.

description: Galuxwadzuwus, the Crooked-Beak of Heaven, is a man-eating bird of the Kwakwaka'wakw winter ceremonial, one of the cannibal attendants of the great devourer Baxbaxwalanuksiwe at the North End of the World. Dancers who wear his long, downward-curving beak mask in the Hamatsa ceremony tame his uncontrolled hunger through ritual.
source: Franz Boas, The Social Organization and the Secret Societies of the Kwakiutl (1897); Kwakwaka'wakw mythology; U'Mista Cultural Centre
research_notes: Attested. Galuxwadzuwus (Crooked-Beak) is a genuine cannibal bird of the Hamatsa society, attendant of Baxbaxwalanuksiwe. Wearing his mask in the Hamatsa dance is a high honor. Matches the input.

description: In the Chinook origin account, an old giantess, wise in the protocols of the spirit world, gave tools and guidance as the South Wind hatched Thunderbird's egg on Saddleback Mountain; the children that emerged became the first Chinook people. research_notes: Attested as a Chinook/Clatsop creation episode. NPS Lewis and Clark materials recount the old giantess, South Wind and the Thunderbird egg that hatched the tribes at Saddle Mountain, including the salmon-slicing taboo. The input aligns.

description: Átsé hashké, 'First Angry,' is the Navajo personification of anger and witchcraft, called into being in the primordial world. In the Origin Myths of the Navaho he stole the children of Water Buffalo by stretching a rainbow across the waters, an act that introduced evil and witchcraft into the world and made him the source of malevolence among the Holy People.

description: Fog Woman is a Tlingit supernatural being who, in Swanton's 'Raven and Fog Woman' (myth #108), was Raven's wife. Washing her hands in a basket, she summoned the first salmon into the world; when Raven grew jealous and cruel, she and the salmon departed to the sea. The story explains the origin of salmon runs and the seasons.

research_notes: Attested. Fog Woman creates the first salmon by washing her hands in a basket and leaves with them when Raven is cruel. Matches the input and Swanton's text.
